board_asks: draw electron-dot (Lewis) structures for simple covalent molecules (H2, O2, N2, CH4, CO2 and compounds such as CH3Cl); give the two reasons - catenation and tetravalency - for carbon's huge number of compounds; define a homologous series and give an example; name a compound and identify its functional group; write balanced equations for combustion, the oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid, addition (hydrogenation), substitution, esterification and saponification, with the correct conditions above the arrow; differentiate ethanol and ethanoic acid by their physical and chemical properties; and explain the cleaning action of soap through micelle formation. Most marks sit in drawing the correct structure and writing the right reaction with its conditions.

big_idea.tagline: One element, millions of compounds - because carbon shares.
big_idea.body: Carbon completes its octet not by giving or taking electrons but by sharing them, forming four strong covalent bonds. Two properties - catenation (carbon-to-carbon chains, branches and rings) and tetravalency - let carbon build an enormous family of compounds. Attach a functional group and a whole homologous series behaves alike, so learning one member teaches you the rest. The chapter's reactions - combustion, oxidation, addition, substitution, esterification and saponification - and the cleaning action of soap all follow from this covalent bonding.

definitions.verbatim: Such bonds which are formed by the sharing of an electron pair between two atoms are known as covalent bonds.
definitions.plain: A bond made by two atoms sharing a pair of electrons so that both attain a filled outer shell - no ions are formed, which is why carbon compounds are poor conductors.

definitions.verbatim: Carbon has the unique ability to form bonds with other atoms of carbon, giving rise to large molecules. This property is called catenation.
definitions.plain: Carbon's ability to bond to other carbon atoms to build long chains, branched chains or rings; the strong C-C bond makes these compounds stable.

definitions.verbatim: Compounds of carbon, which are linked by only single bonds between the carbon atoms are called saturated compounds.
definitions.plain: Carbon compounds with only single C-C bonds (the alkanes); they are generally not very reactive.

definitions.verbatim: Compounds of carbon having double or triple bonds between their carbon atoms are called unsaturated compounds.
definitions.plain: Carbon compounds with at least one C=C or C-triple-C bond (alkenes and alkynes); they are more reactive than saturated compounds.

definitions.verbatim: All these carbon compounds which contain only carbon and hydrogen are called hydrocarbons.
definitions.plain: Compounds of only carbon and hydrogen; the saturated ones are alkanes, the unsaturated ones alkenes (double bond) or alkynes (triple bond).

definitions.verbatim: These heteroatoms and the group containing these confer specific properties to the compound, regardless of the length and nature of the carbon chain and hence are called functional groups.
definitions.plain: An atom or group of atoms (like -OH, -CHO, -COOH) that decides the chemical properties of the compound, whatever the length of the carbon chain.

definitions.verbatim: Hence, such a series of compounds in which the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen in a carbon chain is called a homologous series.
definitions.plain: A family of compounds with the same functional group where each member differs from the next by a -CH2- unit (14 u); members share similar chemical properties and show a gradation in physical properties.

definitions.verbatim: The shared pair of electrons is said to constitute a single covalent bond between the two hydrogen atoms.
Such compounds with identical molecular formula but different structures are called structural isomers.
It is called a substitution reaction because one type of atom or a group of atoms takes the place of another.
We see that some substances are capable of adding oxygen to others. These substances are known as oxidising agents.
This reaction is known as saponification because it is used in the preparation of soap.
clusters of molecules in which the hydrophobic tails are in the interior of the cluster and the ionic ends are on the surface of the cluster. This formation is called a micelle.
Detergents are generally sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chlorides or bromides ions, etc.

concepts.title: Covalent bonding and electron-dot structures
concepts.body: Carbon has four valence electrons and cannot easily gain or lose four, so it shares them, forming four covalent bonds. Show only valence electrons as dots or crosses: a single shared pair is a single bond (H2, CH4), two shared pairs a double bond (O2), three shared pairs a triple bond (N2). Because no ions form, covalent compounds have low melting/boiling points and are poor conductors of electricity.
concepts.tested: 3-mark: draw the electron dot structure of a given molecule (e.g. CH3Cl, CO2, ethanoic acid) and explain the covalent bonding.

concepts.title: Allotropes of carbon
concepts.body: Carbon occurs in different forms with the same chemistry but very different physical properties. In diamond each carbon is bonded to four other carbons in a rigid three-dimensional network, making it the hardest natural substance. In graphite each carbon is bonded to three others in hexagonal layers, so it is soft, slippery and (unusually for a non-metal) a good conductor. Fullerenes are a third class - C-60 has carbon atoms arranged in a football shape.
concepts.tested: 2-mark: compare the structure and one physical property of diamond and graphite; name the C-60 allotrope.

concepts.title: Versatile nature of carbon (catenation + tetravalency)
concepts.body: Two features explain why millions of carbon compounds exist. Catenation is carbon's ability to bond to other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings; the C-C bond is strong and stable because carbon is small. Tetravalency means each carbon can bond to four other atoms - of carbon or of oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur, chlorine and more - giving compounds with many different properties.
concepts.tested: 2-mark: state the two properties of carbon that lead to the huge number of carbon compounds.

concepts.title: Chains, branches, rings and isomers
concepts.body: Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes, methane to hexane) have only single bonds; unsaturated ones have double bonds (alkenes) or triple bonds (alkynes). Carbon skeletons can be straight chains, branched chains or rings (e.g. cyclohexane, benzene). From four carbons onward the same molecular formula can be arranged in more than one way - these are structural isomers (e.g. two isomers of butane, C4H10).
concepts.tested: 3-mark: draw the structures/structural isomers of a named compound (e.g. the isomers of pentane) and classify as saturated or unsaturated.

concepts.title: Homologous series, functional groups and naming
concepts.body: Replacing a hydrogen on a carbon chain with a functional group (halo-, alcohol -OH, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid) fixes the chemistry of the compound. A homologous series shares one functional group, with successive members differing by a -CH2- unit (14 u); chemical properties stay similar while melting/boiling points rise gradually. To name a compound: count the carbons for the stem (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-...), then add the group's prefix or suffix, dropping the final 'e' before a vowel suffix (propane - e + one = propanone).
concepts.tested: 3-mark: define a homologous series with an example; name compounds or identify the functional group from a formula.

concepts.title: Chemical properties of carbon compounds
concepts.body: Combustion: carbon and its compounds burn in oxygen to give carbon dioxide (and water) with heat and light; saturated hydrocarbons give a clean blue flame, unsaturated ones a sooty yellow flame. Oxidation: alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by oxidising agents (alkaline KMnO4 or acidified K2Cr2O7). Addition: unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen over a nickel/palladium catalyst (hydrogenation). Substitution: in sunlight, chlorine replaces the hydrogens of a saturated hydrocarbon one by one.
concepts.tested: identify the reaction type from an equation; name the products; state which hydrocarbons undergo addition reactions.

concepts.title: Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents
concepts.body: Ethanol (alcohol) reacts with sodium to release hydrogen and, with hot concentrated sulphuric acid, dehydrates to ethene. Ethanoic acid (acetic acid, a weak carboxylic acid; its pure form is glacial acetic acid) forms an ester with ethanol (esterification), gives a salt and water with a base, and releases carbon dioxide with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates. Soaps are sodium/potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids; their molecules form micelles that trap oily dirt (ionic heads out, hydrocarbon tails in) so it rinses away, while detergents keep working even in hard water.
concepts.tested: 3-mark: explain the cleaning action of soap via micelle formation; differentiate ethanol and ethanoic acid by their properties.

examples.shape: Oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid
examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] Why is the conversion of ethanol to ethanoic acid an oxidation reaction, and which reagent brings it about?

solution_steps.text: Oxygen is added to ethanol, turning the alcohol into a carboxylic acid - addition of oxygen is oxidation.
Alkaline potassium permanganate (or acidified potassium dichromate) supplies the oxygen; such substances are oxidising agents:

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark: oxygen is added to ethanol so it is oxidation (1) + naming the oxidising agent, alkaline KMnO4 or acidified K2Cr2O7 (1).

examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] What is hydrogenation? Give the catalyst used and one industrial application.

solution_steps.text: Hydrogenation is an addition reaction in which unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen over a nickel (or palladium) catalyst to give saturated hydrocarbons:
It is used to convert unsaturated vegetable oils into saturated fats (vegetable ghee) using a nickel catalyst.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark: defining hydrogenation as the catalytic addition of hydrogen to unsaturated hydrocarbons (1) + its industrial use, hardening vegetable oils to fats over a Ni catalyst (1).

examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] Methane reacts with chlorine in the presence of sunlight. Write the equation and explain why it is called a substitution reaction.

solution_steps.text: In sunlight, chlorine replaces the hydrogen atoms of the saturated hydrocarbon one by one:
It is a substitution reaction because one type of atom (chlorine) takes the place of another (hydrogen).

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark: the balanced substitution equation of methane with chlorine in sunlight (1) + the reason, a chlorine atom substitutes for a hydrogen atom (1).

examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol and a little concentrated sulphuric acid. Name the reaction and product, write the equation, and state what happens when the product is treated with sodium hydroxide.

solution_steps.text: Ethanoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of an acid catalyst to form a sweet-smelling ester:
The ester (ethyl ethanoate) is sweet-smelling and is used in perfumes and as a flavouring agent.
On heating with sodium hydroxide the ester is converted back to the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid - this is saponification, used to prepare soap:

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark: naming esterification and the balanced ester-forming equation (1.5) + the ester's use as a perfume/flavour (0.5) + saponification with NaOH giving the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid (1).

examples.shape: Ethanoic acid with a base and a carbonate
examples.problem_verbatim: [authored prompt] How does ethanoic acid react with (i) sodium hydroxide and (ii) sodium carbonate? Write the balanced equations and name the gas evolved in (ii).

solution_steps.text: Like a mineral acid it neutralises sodium hydroxide to give a salt (sodium acetate) and water:
With sodium carbonate it gives the salt, water and carbon dioxide gas:
The gas evolved in (ii) is carbon dioxide, which turns freshly prepared lime-water milky.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark: the neutralisation equation with NaOH giving sodium acetate + water (1) + the equation with sodium carbonate giving salt + water + CO2 (1) + identifying the gas as carbon dioxide by the lime-water test (1).

strategies.text: Show only the valence electrons and give every atom a completely filled outer shell. Carbon is tetravalent, so it forms four shared pairs; one shared pair is a single bond, two pairs a double bond, three pairs a triple bond.

First count the carbon atoms for the stem (meth-1, eth-2, prop-3, but-4...), then add the functional group as a prefix or suffix. Drop the final 'e' of the stem before a suffix beginning with a vowel (propane - e + one = propanone).
Saturated + Cl2 in sunlight is substitution; unsaturated + H2 over Ni is addition; alcohol + oxidising agent is oxidation; acid + alcohol is esterification; ester + NaOH is saponification.

Explain the soap molecule's two ends (an ionic hydrophilic head and a hydrocarbon hydrophobic tail), how micelles form around oily dirt, and how agitation lifts the emulsified dirt into the water so it rinses away.

pitfalls.text: Changing subscripts instead of coefficients to balance a combustion equation - only the coefficients in front of a formula may be changed, never the subscripts inside it.
Confusing addition (hydrogen adds across the double/triple bond of an unsaturated compound) with substitution (an atom replaces a hydrogen in a saturated compound).
Forgetting to drop the final 'e' of the stem before a vowel suffix - e.g. writing 'propaneone' instead of propanone.
Claiming a micelle forms in any solvent. It forms in water because one end is hydrophilic; in a pure hydrocarbon solvent no micelle forms.
Calling ethanoic acid a strong acid. Carboxylic acids are weak acids and are only partially ionised, unlike mineral acids such as HCl.

third_tab_content.intro: For Chemistry the subject-adaptive third tab holds the chapter's key reactions - the formal core you must be able to reproduce, grouped by property. Every reaction is a real NCERT Ch 4 reaction; the condition sits above/beside the arrow. Where NCERT prints a skeletal equation and asks you to balance it, the balanced form is given and flagged.

reactions.name: Combustion - carbon
reactions.equation: C + O2 -> CO2 + heat and light
reactions.conditions: Carbon burns completely in oxygen; an oxidation reaction

reactions.name: Combustion - methane
reactions.conditions: Balanced form of the skeletal combustion equation printed on p.69

reactions.name: Combustion - ethanol
reactions.conditions: Balanced form of the skeletal combustion equation printed on p.69; alcohol burns cleanly

reactions.name: Oxidation - ethanol to ethanoic acid
reactions.equation: CH3CH2OH --Alkaline KMnO4 + heat / Acidified K2Cr2O7 + heat--> CH3COOH
reactions.conditions: Alcohol oxidised to carboxylic acid; the oxidising agent adds oxygen

reactions.name: Addition - hydrogenation of unsaturated hydrocarbons
reactions.conditions: Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen over a Ni/Pd catalyst to give saturated hydrocarbons; used to harden vegetable oils (NCERT describes this reaction textually, p.71)

reactions.name: Substitution - methane and chlorine
reactions.conditions: In sunlight chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms of the saturated hydrocarbon one by one

reactions.name: Ethanol with sodium
reactions.conditions: Alcohols react with sodium; hydrogen gas is evolved and sodium ethoxide is formed

reactions.name: Dehydration of ethanol to ethene
reactions.equation: CH3CH2OH --Hot conc. H2SO4, 443 K--> CH2=CH2 + H2O
reactions.conditions: Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent, giving the unsaturated ethene

reactions.name: Esterification
reactions.conditions: Acid + alcohol give a sweet-smelling ester (ethyl ethanoate) and water; acid catalyst

reactions.name: Saponification
reactions.conditions: Ester + alkali give the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid; the basis of soap-making

reactions.name: Ethanoic acid with a base
reactions.conditions: Neutralisation; gives sodium ethanoate (sodium acetate) and water

reactions.name: Ethanoic acid with sodium carbonate
reactions.conditions: Gives salt + water + carbon dioxide (turns lime-water milky)
